items.title: Fresh tanker attack in Hormuz highlights ongoing threats facing Gulf shipping
items.original_title: Fresh tanker attack in Hormuz highlights ongoing threats facing Gulf shipping
items.summary: A new tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz has been reported by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre, in the latest of a string of incidents targeting vessels attempting to traverse the vital waterway. In a statement dated Monday, the British trade monitor said a third-party had reported that the attack had disabled the ship and sparked a fire in the engine room. The crew are reportedly safe, while the damage assessment and environmental impact of the attack was unknown. The UKMTO reiterated a recent warning that vessels should transit Hormuz with “caution.” Since November 10, the UKMTO has reported seven attacks in or near Hormuz, a key conduit for roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the outbreak of the Iran war in late February. Despite moves by Iran to stem traffic through Hormuz, shipping data have indicated that more tankers are making the sailing thanks in part to increase U.S. security in the region. Still, the attacks have sustained fears of possible disruptions to oil flows out of the Gulf region, while messaging around negotiations to end the Middle East conflict has been muddled.

items.title: Fuel Switch Snapshot: LSMGO undercuts LNG and LBM for diesel SS engines
items.original_title: Fuel Switch Snapshot: LSMGO undercuts LNG and LBM for diesel SS engines
items.summary: A $102/mt drop in Rotterdam’s LSMGO over the past week has made the conventional fuel grade cheaper than both LNG and liquefied biomethane (LBM) in the port for vessels with diesel slow speed (diesel SS) engines. LNG prices have dipped $8-9/mt and LBM prices have fallen $13-14/mt depending on engine type in the same period. LNG burnt in diesel SS engines has flipped from a $78/mt discount to LSMGO to a $15/mt premium over the past week. LNG’s premium over LSMGO has widened by $94/mt to $122/mt for Otto MS engines, and LBM’s by $89/mt to $174/mt. For vessels with diesel SS engines, it has narrowed by $5/mt to $47/mt. Singapore’s LNG prices have fallen by $131/mt for both engine types, as the JKM contract they are priced on has moved from December to January delivery, a move that accounts for $75/mt of the fall and leaves both down by $56/mt without it. For vessels with Otto MS engines, LNG’s premium over LSMGO in Singapore has narrowed by $136/mt to $141/mt. For vessels with diesel SS engines, it has narrowed by $136/mt to $88/mt. LNG’s premium over B100 for vessels with diesel SS engines has narrowed by $117/mt to just $3/mt over the past week.

items.original_title: SFL expands Orca AI deployment following successful initial rollout
items.summary: International shipowner and charterer SFL Corporation Ltd. is expanding Orca AI across 44 vessels, establishing a common approach to navigational safety as its portfolio grows. The agreement covers vessels across SFL’s growing portfolio, as well as future newbuilds and vessels added through S&P activities. From initial deployment to broader adoption SFL began working with Orca AI in 2025 through an initial deployment across five vessels. Over the following year, teams across Europe and Asia tested Orca AI in real operations, combining onboard trials with direct feedback from crews, technical managers, and shore teams. One operational view across ship and shore Across SFL’s portfolio, Orca AI connects the navigational picture onboard with how safety events are understood ashore. This shared view helps SFL identify recurring risks and turn events from daily operations into fleetwide safety learning. We are still in the early days, and SFL wants to take part in that development.” Orca AI Co-founder and CEO Yarden Gross added: “SFL combines the commercial discipline of an established shipowner with a willingness to embrace new technology. Its decision to invest in AI-assisted navigation on this scale sends a strong signal to the wider industry, and we’re proud to be working with a company prepared to help lead that change.” Source: Orca AI

items.title: How the Hormuz crisis handed America a lasting export advantage
items.original_title: How the Hormuz crisis handed America a lasting export advantage
items.summary: As Middle Eastern supplies faltered, American exporters of LNG, LPG, jet fuel and plastics gained new customers, new shipping routes and, in some cases, contracts stretching decades into the future. Alex Byelyavtsev reports. When the Strait of Hormuz became unreliable in 2026, some of the world’s largest suppliers of energy and industrial materials lost their normal access to customers overseas. Enterprise Products Partners was already expanding propane and butane export capacity at its Houston Ship Channel terminal by another 300,000 barrels a day, illustrating how established American terminals were positioned to handle greater demand. A buyer who previously received propane from the Persian Gulf might now need a gas carrier to collect it in Texas. According to US government energy data, jet-fuel exports averaged 356,000 barrels a day in the second quarter of 2026, more than double the five-year average. Plastics and resins accounted for about 45% of Port Houston’s containerised export teu in 2025. Across the United States, exporters booked more than 6,000 containers of plastic materials in a single day in March, well above normal levels. Its contract is secure, the cargo is available, and a ship can be arranged.

items.title: StealthGas crew airlifted from stricken LPG carrier off Bulgaria
items.original_title: StealthGas crew airlifted from stricken LPG carrier off Bulgaria
items.summary: All 19 crewmembers of a StealthGas LPG carrier have been rescued after the vessel was caught up in a suspected drone attack off Bulgaria, the second serious merchant shipping incident in the western Black Sea in less than 24 hours. The Liberia-flagged, 7,500 cu m Gas Husky got into trouble overnight on Monday while sailing from Alexandria, Egypt, towards Romania’s Midia port. The 2012-built vessel disappeared from tracking systems shortly after midnight, with its emergency position-indicating radio beacon activated around 8 am local time on Tuesday. The 7,218 dwt fully pressurised LPG carrier forms part of Harry Vafias-led StealthGas’s fleet. The ship was approximately 14.5 nautical miles from the location where the Somali-flagged general cargo vessel Betul 8 capsized on Monday. That vessel, carrying around 3,000 tonnes of wheat from Romania to Egypt, was reportedly struck by two unmanned surface vessels before taking on water. All 12 crewmembers were rescued in an operation involving Bulgarian, Romanian and Turkish forces. Maritime security consultancy Diaplous has recorded at least 17 merchant vessels attacked off Romania and Bulgaria since mid-July, with several casualties reported in recent weeks. The latest incidents have occurred close to shipping routes used by vessels trading to and from Ukrainian and Romanian Black Sea ports.

items.title: Gemini carriers target complete return to Suez transits by mid-January
items.original_title: Gemini carriers target complete return to Suez transits by mid-January
items.summary: Gemini Cooperation partners Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd will have made a full resumption of Suez transits on their Asia-Europe services by mid-January. Yesterday, the partners outlined the schedule for the last three Asia-North Europe services still detouring via the Cape of Good Hope to return to the Red Sea routing. The Asia-Northern Europe Loop 1 (Maersk AE2/Hapag-Lloyd NE1) will resume Suez transits in both directions with the departure of the 18,300 teu Mary Maersk from Ningbo on 4 December. The Asia-Northern Europe Loop 3 (Maersk AE3/Hapag-Lloyd NE3) will also fully resume westbound Suez transits following the departure of the 16,300 teu Alette Maersk from Shanghai on 20 December. Meanwhile, shippers on the Asia-Northern Europe Loop 2 (Maersk AE1/Hapag-Lloyd NE2), operated entirely by Hagag-Lloyd vessels, will have to wait until early 2027, with a full westbound resumption beginning with the departure of the 23,700 teu Damietta Express from Shanghai on 14 January, representing the last of Gemini’s Asia-Europe strings to return to Suez. It also remains to be seen how the widespread return to Suez routings will impact Asia-Europe schedule reliability, which according to Xeneta data, has fallen to historic lows – just 4% of vessels arrived on time in Europe ex-Asia in September, which rose to 7% in October.

The MIT–Mecalux research, involving 1,967 supply chain and warehousing professionals across 21 countries, found 83% had already reported accelerating AI adoption in the past year. The study also found that 40% of organisations had abandoned at least one AI initiative over the past two years – integration difficulties, poor data quality, and disappointing returns among the principal reasons. It will focus on automating labour-intensive, high-mix, low-volume value-added services (VAS), including kitting, labelling, and packing, using robotics, AI vision systems, and connected automation. items.title: Box ship charter rates still climbing as lines hunt for more tonnage
items.original_title: Box ship charter rates still climbing as lines hunt for more tonnage
items.summary: Charter prices for containerships continue to defy the cooldown in long-haul freight rates, as major operators continue to hunt tonnage. Linerlytica this week reported that French line CMA CGM took the 2001-built 5,610 teu Aigio (previously known as Wan Hai 611 ) for 3.5 years. While the rate was not disclosed, charter rates for similar-size vessels are around $66,000 a day, up 10% year on year. Aigio is one of three sister ships Wan Hai sold in March for $34m to $38m each, Greek tonnage provider Costamare buying two and CMA CGM the other – Wan Hai 612 and Wan Hai 613 have not been renamed or delivered yet. Charter rates for box ships of all sizes have risen by between 7% and 23% year on year, with feeder vessels registering the biggest gains due to higher demand from intra-region trades and the lack of newbuilds in recent years. A 1,700 teu ship is now going for around $32,000 a day. “The strong demand in the containership charter market continues, with charter rates still edging upwards, with forward fixtures stretching into the end of 2027,” Linerlytica said. Meanwhile MSC, by far the busiest buyer of second-hand ships, continues to hunt for tonnage to consolidate its lead over its peers.

items.title: More pain for India-Gulf shippers as costly box returns add to rising rates
items.original_title: More pain for India-Gulf shippers as costly box returns add to rising rates
items.summary: Apart from the lingering pressure of ocean freight rates that remain stubbornly elevated, India-Middle East shippers are facing various extra cost shocks, due to shifting carriers’ cargo handling policies and landside supply chain hurdles in the conflict region. According to industry sources, fresh booking curbs imposed by mainline operators like Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have further constrained capacity options for India’s cargo flows to the Persian Gulf. With available vessel space from JNPA (Nhava Sheva) and Mundra to Khor Fakkan and Fujairah in the UAE, and Sohar in Oman, becoming tighter and more erratic, rates for these “lifeline” port pairs have risen from the levels seen last month, data suggests. Spot rates offered by CMA CGM for JNPA to Khor Fakkan are around $7,500 per 40ft, compared with $6,500 to $7,000 in the second half of October. “With fewer sailings, active capacity providers have the room to adjust rates dynamically.” Rates ex-India to the other Gulf ports of discharge have also climbed month on month because of the supply-side issues, sources said. CMA CGM’s spot rates for a 40ft booking from JNPA to Sohar are around $6,500, nearly double what the carrier was quoting at the end of September. And the Gulf trade pain for shippers goes beyond soaring ocean rates.

items.summary: Goldman Sachs forecasts European natural gas prices could reach 150 EUR/MWh in the first quarter of 2027 under specific supply and weather conditions, according to a research note released by the firm. The investment bank projects TTF prices could rally near that level if Persian Gulf liquefied natural gas exports average 25-30% of pre-war levels this winter and Europe experiences a winter that is one standard deviation colder than average, or 0.7°C below normal temperatures. Under a separate scenario where Gulf LNG exports remain at approximately 35% of pre-war levels through the end of 2027, Goldman Sachs estimates TTF prices would average 104 EUR/MWh in 2027. The projections appear in Exhibit 6 of the firm’s analysis on European Union gas prices. The forecasts link European gas price movements to the level of LNG export recovery from the Persian Gulf region. TTF refers to the Title Transfer Facility, the pricing benchmark for natural gas traded in Europe. Source: Investing.com

items.title: African nations join forces to impose carbon charges on shipping
items.original_title: African nations join forces to impose carbon charges on shipping
items.summary: A growing group of African nations is pushing ahead with plans to introduce carbon charges on international shipping, raising the prospect of another regional emissions regime for shipowners already grappling with European environmental legislation. Guinea, Ivory Coast and Mauritania have signed an agreement at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, to develop a coordinated approach to charging ships for their carbon emissions. The initiative, promoted by the Africa Sovereign Carbon Registry Foundation (ASCRF), builds on existing schemes in Djibouti and Gabon, with the ambition of establishing a continent-wide framework for raising climate finance from international shipping and aviation. Under the model pioneered by Djibouti, vessels are charged $17 per tonne of CO2 calculated on 50% of emissions from voyages to and from the country’s ports. The latest agreement brings the number of countries associated with the proposed African coalition to six, although the status of Liberia’s involvement remains contentious. Monrovia stated earlier this year that it would not impose a unilateral carbon levy on international shipping. Other African countries are considering similar schemes. The development comes at a particularly sensitive moment for shipping’s decarbonisation negotiations, with the International Maritime Organization due to resume discussions on its proposed global emissions framework later this month.

items.title: EU widens shadow fleet crackdown to tanker managers and oil buyers
items.original_title: EU widens shadow fleet crackdown to tanker managers and oil buyers
items.summary: The European Union has widened its sanctions campaign against Russia’s shadow fleet, targeting tanker owners, shipmanagers, insurers and oil buyers across several countries in a fresh effort to disrupt Moscow’s seaborne energy exports. The measures adopted on Monday add 12 individuals and 101 entities to the EU’s sanctions lists, including companies in the UAE, China, Seychelles and Oman involved in trading Russian oil. Among those targeted are Dubai-based Lidoil DMCC, Spikoil DMCC, Lynx Ship Management, Stalwart Shipmanagement, Grace Shipmanagement and Greenlight Shipmanagement. The crackdown extends to JSC Petersburg Oil Terminal, which operates oil export infrastructure in the St Petersburg region. Nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions have also been sanctioned, tightening restrictions on the financing of the country’s energy trade. The measures impose asset freezes and prohibit EU businesses from providing funds or economic resources to the designated entities. The latest action follows Britain’s blacklisting of 11 additional vessels last week and comes amid intensifying European scrutiny of Russia’s international tanker operations. France and Britain will host an international conference in Paris on December 4 to coordinate further action against the shadow fleet. More than 670 vessels are already subject to EU port access and maritime services restrictions.

All 12 crewmembers were rescued by helicopter following a multinational operation involving Bulgarian, Romanian and Turkish naval vessels. Bulgarian authorities have yet to confirm the cause or establish who was responsible.< Maritime security consultancy Diaplous now counts 17 merchant vessels attacked off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria since mid-July. The facility can process approximately 6.6m tonnes of crude annually. items.title: China emerges as dry bulk export powerhouse
items.original_title: China emerges as dry bulk export powerhouse
items.summary: China’s transformation from the world’s dominant dry bulk importer into an increasingly significant exporter is gathering pace, with outbound cargo volumes more than doubling since 2020 and accounting for nearly two-thirds of global dry bulk shipment growth this year. New analysis from Ursa Shipbrokers, using Signal Ocean vessel-tracking data, shows Chinese dry bulk loadings reached 274.9m tonnes in the first 10 months of 2026, up 14.9% year-on-year China accounted for 35.6m tonnes of the 54.4m-tonne increase in global dry bulk loadings during the period, an extraordinary contribution from a country traditionally viewed principally as a destination for raw materials. Its share of worldwide dry bulk loadings has climbed from just 2.5% in 2020 to 5.5% this year, with annual export shipments rising from 128.6m tonnes to 291.5m tonnes between 2020 and 2025. “From being an almost sole importer of dry cargoes [China] has emerged into a large exporter over the last few years, a very interesting development indeed,” Ivar Hansson Myklebust, chairman and chief executive of Norwegian owner Belships, told Splash in an interview last week. Cement and clinker exports have climbed from negligible levels to around 25m tonnes in just a few years. Steel remains another major export commodity.

items.title: Hong Kong’s shipowner dynasties face the succession test
items.original_title: Hong Kong’s shipowner dynasties face the succession test
items.summary: The city’s great shipping families have survived every imaginable market shock. Keeping the next generation – and its capital – anchored in Hong Kong may prove a different challenge. The latest chapter from our brand new Hong Kong magazine, which is being distributed across the city’s maritime week. Hong Kong’s commercial memory includes the failures as well as the fortunes. Firoze Mirza, chairman of BSM Hong Kong, observes that several established families now have “third and fourth generations in the saddle”. Vikrant Gusain, chief executive of Dockendale Group, puts the succession challenge sharply: “Shipping therefore has to compete for family capital rather than assume it will inherit it.” More importantly, he argues, the next generation must be able to build a modern shipping enterprise in Hong Kong, not simply administer ships acquired by their parents or grandparents. Hong Kong-listed Pacific Basin moved strategic leadership and commercial decision-making to Singapore in 2025 amid US-China port-fee tensions, while Seaspan also relocated its headquarters to the city-state. The threat, therefore, is not an imminent extinction of Hong Kong’s shipping families. If the next generation continues to own vessels but chooses to finance, charter and direct them elsewhere, Hong Kong can retain impressive maritime statistics while losing some of the commercial influence that made those statistics possible.

An example in Terminal Activity Using the Terminal Activity workspace in Container Intelligence, we can take four carrier groups calling San Pedro, Seattle, and Tacoma on vessels above 5,000 TEU, benchmarked against each other from January through September 2026: MSC is the dominant carrier at these ports by volume, with 122 terminal calls across the period, more than the other three carrier groups combined. China COSCO Shipping: 6.4 hours waiting plus 35.9 hours at berth, roughly 42 hours per call, the shortest total of the four. The carrier with the best waiting numbers has, by a wide margin, the longest total time in port once berth stay is counted. items.title: Onboard carbon capture: a practical pathway for shipping?
items.original_title: Onboard carbon capture: a practical pathway for shipping?

Energy-efficiency measures reduce fuel consumption, but even those more efficient crossings will continue to produce carbon emissions. A potential role opens for onboard carbon capture and storage (oCCS). Eastern Pacific Shipping’s Pacific Cobalt became the first classed commercial oCCS installation in 2024 under LR’s Emission Abatement Carbon Capture & Storage (EACCS) (Amine, HFO) class notation, while Solvang’s Clipper Eris is testing a full-scale system designed to capture around 70% of the CO₂ produced by its main engine. For the right vessel types and trades, it offers a realistic pathway to reducing CO₂ emissions and managing carbon costs while fuel supply chains, infrastructure and regulations continue to evolve.” The strongest opportunities for oCCS are likely to be those vessels with sufficient remaining trading life and space for the equipment. The IMO is still developing a global framework covering safety, testing, verification and carbon accounting. Entering an oCCS world oCCS could offer an emissions-reduction pathway for suitable vessels using fossil fuels or their artificial equivalents as the transition to zero and near-zero emission fuels develops. Regulation also needs to recognise the resulting emissions reduction, to help create a working carbon economy.

items.summary: Cargo ships are seen from a patrol boat of Ukraine’s coast guard as they sail in the Black Sea, amid Russia’s attack on Ukraine, February 7, 2024. REUTERS/Thomas Peter A Somali-flagged cargo ship carrying nearly 3,000 metric tons of wheat capsized off Bulgaria on Monday after what crew members described as an attack by two sea drones, marking the latest in a growing series of strikes against commercial shipping in the Black Sea. All 12 crew members aboard the BETUL 8 were rescued in an operation involving Bulgarian military helicopters and naval vessels from Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey. Bulgarian maritime news outlet Maritime.bg , which spoke with surviving crew members, reported that two unmanned surface vessels struck the ship before it capsized. items.title: How reliable in predicting spot prices is box ship utilisation?
items.original_title: How reliable in predicting spot prices is box ship utilisation?
items.summary: The relationship between vessel utilisation and container spot freight rates is markedly different on the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades. New analysis from Sea-Intelligence raises questions over how reliably capacity utilisation can predict pricing. The analyst found a strong correlation between utilisation and spot rates on the transpacific, where freight rates rise sharply once vessel utilisation exceeds 90%. On the transpacific, the analysis identified a clear relationship between utilisation and freight rates, with the strongest correlation, 71%, occurring when spot rates lagged changes in utilisation by one month. A further analysis of utilisation against spot rates showed freight rates begin climbing steeply once utilisation passes 90%, reflecting a tightening capacity market in which shippers compete for available slots. Its correlation analysis and scatter plot showed changes in nominal vessel utilisation were a poor indicator of spot rate movements on the trade, which the analyst suggested reflected fundamental differences in the structure of the two trades. On the transpacific, most vessel capacity is dedicated to cargo moving between Asia and North America, making utilisation a relatively direct measure of the balance between supply and demand, while Asia-Europe is more complex, as vessels carry cargo for multiple markets through major transhipment hubs along their routes.

items.summary: The LNG spot market saw a mixed week, with the East remaining active and rates holding at a premium to the Atlantic. In the Atlantic, activity picked up across the US Gulf and West Africa, but extensive vessel availability and subdued cargo liquidity continue to limit upside. On the BLNG1 Australia–Japan route, 174k cbm vessels edged up $200 week-on-week to settle at $54,600/day, supported by continued enquiry and a tighter tonnage list, especially for 2-Stroke vessels. In the time-charter market, the six-month rate held steady at $44,200/day, while the one-year term eased $1,167 to $52,900/day. Reduced cargo economics and softer fixing interest contributed to a general downward correction in freight rates. The BLPG1 Ras Tanura–Chiba route settled at $251.20/tonne, with TCE earnings closing at $245,894/day. The BLPG2 Houston–Flushing route weakened by $6.33 week-on-week to settle at $174.50/tonne, with TCE earnings falling $8,401 to $205,311/day. Growing vessel availability contributed to the downward pressure. Similarly, the BLPG3 Houston–Chiba route declined by $11.86 to close at $310.86/tonne, while TCE returns dropped $8,172 to settle at $190,386/day, reflecting the weakening sentiment in the Atlantic market.

items.title: Himalaya secures fresh 2027 charter cover for newcastlemax pair
items.original_title: Himalaya secures fresh 2027 charter cover for newcastlemax pair
items.summary: Tor Olav Trøim-backed Himalaya Shipping has switched two of its newcastlemax bulkers from index-linked employment to fixed-rate charters averaging $41,550 per day for the first quarter of 2027. The Oslo- and New York-listed owner said the rate locks will run from January 1 through March 31, securing approximately $7.5m in gross hire across the two vessels over the three-month period. The latest move adds to a series of charter conversions this year. In August, the company fixed two newcastlemaxes at an average $51,200 per day through December, followed by another two at $53,000 per day from September through March 2027. Earlier this month, Himalaya also secured fresh employment for two vessels with their existing charterer, extending the contracts until at least October 2027, with a three-year evergreen structure thereafter. Those agreements remain index-linked at premiums to the Baltic 5TC capesize benchmark. The Lars-Christian Svensen-led company operates a fleet of 12 LNG dual-fuel, 210,000 dwt newcastlemaxes delivered between 2023 and 2024. Himalaya reported average gross time charter equivalent earnings of $58,400 per day in the third quarter, compared with an average Baltic 5TC 180 Capesize Index of $41,369.

items.title: Why a collision with no deaths got more attention than two wars at sea
items.original_title: Why a collision with no deaths got more attention than two wars at sea
items.summary: Dustin Eno, a crisis communications consultant, and founder of the Maritime Attention Index, gives his take on Friday’s high-profile allision in New Orleans. On Friday November 13, Iran said an LNG tanker had hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz and exploded. That afternoon in New Orleans, the tanker Atlantic Asphalt ran into the river cruise ship American Heritage at her berth on the Mississippi and capsized her. Compare that with the two wars being fought at sea. So why did the wars lose the attention battle this weekend? The allision (collision with a stationary object) was filmed by several people, from several angles, at every stage — the tanker coming in, the impact, the riverboat going over, passengers swimming to safety. An attack in the Gulf or the Black Sea usually reaches us as a statement from a navy or a ministry, perhaps with a photo of smoke on the horizon taken hours later. When tankers were hit in Hormuz at the start of this month, it stayed below 80, and a drone sinking a cargo ship off Romania in October barely moved it. Most reports refer only to “the tanker’s owners”, and mostly because the Port of New Orleans is now suing them for more than $1m.

items.title: Safer Ship-to-Ship Transfers: Practical Lessons for Bulk Carrier Operations
items.original_title: Safer Ship-to-Ship Transfers: Practical Lessons for Bulk Carrier Operations
items.summary: Ship-to-ship (STS) transfer operations are an established part of dry bulk shipping, particularly where draught restrictions, limited port infrastructure or the absence of a suitable berth make direct loading or discharge impracticable. However, bringing two vessels alongside to transfer cargo introduces risks that differ considerably from conventional terminal operations. INTERCARGO’s Ship to Ship Transfer Guidelines for Bulk Carriers provides practical guidance specifically for the dry bulk sector, covering operations between bulk carriers as well as transfers involving barges, transloaders, floating cranes and transshipment units. The fact that two vessels are individually capable of conducting STS operations does not necessarily mean they are suitable for operating alongside each other. Roles, responsibilities, communication channels and emergency signals should be clearly understood before operations commence. Use the guidance as a working tool One of the most useful aspects of INTERCARGO’s publication is its practical material. It also contains practical information on fender selection, mooring arrangements and cargo operations. A useful resource for Members Bulk carrier STS operations bring together vessel compatibility, mooring, fendering, cargo handling, stability, environmental conditions and human factors within a single operation.

items.title: IMO faces challenges in net-zero framework compliance without emissions cost
items.original_title: IMO faces challenges in net-zero framework compliance without emissions cost
items.summary: Countries are struggling to design rules to make shipping companies comply with a new bunker regulation designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, a senior International Bunker Industry Association official said Nov. 12, as Washington leads opposition to financial punitive measures. International Maritime Organization member states, having failed to adopt the Net-Zero Framework as scheduled in October 2025, are due to meet again between Nov. “The sticking point is on the financial aspects.” In its current form, the framework is composed of GHG intensity thresholds for marine energy that tighten progressively over 2028-2035, and financial costs for shipping companies failing to meet the standards. Compliance mechanism Countries supporting the current net-zero framework have designed the financial element to promote the use of low-carbon marine fuels, which remain much more costly than conventional, oil-based fuels due to limited availability. October’s average delivered bunker costs for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil are $22.78 per gigajoule in Singapore, compared with $27/GJ for bioblend B24, $28.48/GJ for LNG, and $48.47/GJ for 100% sustainable methanol, according to the Platts global bunker cost calculator. “You need some way of closing that price gap.” The IBIA official said challenges lie ahead for member states on how to design an alternative compliance mechanism if the current net-zero framework is to be revised.

items.title: Even with a durable ceasefire, these factors will support oil prices: BCA
items.original_title: Even with a durable ceasefire, these factors will support oil prices: BCA
items.summary: BCA Research says oil’s recent sell-off has largely removed the war premium from prices, leaving the risks skewed to the upside. The firm expects Brent crude to trade in a range of $90 to $110 per barrel. “Oil’s month-to-date selloff has priced out much of the war premium,” BCA wrote. “Investors should not treat a rapid resolution to the conflict as a foregone conclusion,” the firm said. With the risk premium already compressed, BCA said a peace deal would push prices down only modestly, while a meaningful escalation would send them to fresh highs for the conflict. It added that depleted inventories would offer less of a cushion in a renewed disruption, as governments focus on conserving stockpiles rather than releasing them aggressively. Even in a durable ceasefire, BCA expects support for prices. Gulf producers are likely to maximize output and exports while conditions allow, but the firm said recovering demand, including Chinese imports, along with efforts to rebuild inventories, should absorb the extra barrels. “This creates a floor for Brent, even in the event of a durable ceasefire,” BCA said.

China has also confirmed, on 9 November 2026, that the suspension of the reciprocal Special Port Fees on US-linked vessels has been further extended up to 10 January 2027. items.original_title: VLCC Deliveries Rise Fivefold as the Orderbook Builds
items.summary: VLCC supply is starting to arrive. After a sharp rise in ordering, the first of the new tonnage is reaching the water, with deliveries already well ahead of last year. Using VesselsValue data, we look at what is on order, who is building it, and why owners keep ordering at near-record prices. Overall, 27.3% of the VLCC fleet is on order. China sits at the centre of VLCC deliveries China holds 268 of the VLCCs on order, c.77% of the orderbook, and builds 106 of the 125 units, due in 2028. Why demand is holding up despite high prices and a large orderbook Replacement alone does not explain it, as the 349 VLCCs on order or launched compares with 183 vessels aged 20 years and above. Of the 932 VLCCs in the fleet, 45.8% are 15 years or older, including 183 vessels aged 20 years and above. VLCC deliveries continue to build Taken together, the data points to a VLCC fleet that is about to grow at a pace not seen in recent years, with the build programme concentrated in China and delivery volumes weighted to 2028 and 2029. Should conditions change, the ageing fleet offers a sizeable pool of tonnage that could leave the market, so the balance between deliveries and demolition will be one to watch.

items.title: India eases flag rules in push for more tonnage
items.original_title: India eases flag rules in push for more tonnage
items.summary: India has relaxed its ship registration rules, allowing vessels with majority Indian ownership to qualify for the national flag in a move that opens the door to foreign minority investment. The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has set the ownership threshold at more than 50%, replacing the full qualifying Indian ownership requirement imposed under the previous Merchant Shipping Act. A government notification published in the Gazette of India sets out the new conditions under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. The threshold applies to legal ownership of shares in the vessel itself, rather than simply the shareholding of a company operating it. Where a non-resident Indian or overseas citizen of India holds the majority interest, an authorised representative based or incorporated in India must be appointed. Owners should still complete the registration process and obtain approval from the authorities. The move comes during a wider push by New Delhi to increase Indian-flagged tonnage and strengthen its domestic shipping industry. Splash reported last year that MSC, Maersk and CMA CGM were looking to shift vessels onto the Indian register, while Hapag-Lloyd signed agreements with the government in March covering possible reflagging of up to four ships. India is also building out its state-backed Bharat Container Shipping Line and has launched initiatives targeting ship finance, insurance and domestic shipbuilding.

items.summary: A drone view of cars, ready to be loaded onto a ship, at the car terminal in port in Durban, South Africa, July 9, 2025. REUTERS/Rogan Ward Nov 14, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Severe delays at South Africa’s biggest container terminal in the port city of Durban are threatening the nation’s auto industry, already under strain from a tide of cheap Asian imports and US tariffs. While Durban has long been among the world’s worst-performing container ports, the government sought to address that through the introduction of a private operator in January. Nearly half the market value of Metair Investments Ltd., a local parts manufacturer supplying Volkswagen, Ford and Toyota, was wiped out on Friday after it warned that port backlogs approaching 20 days threatened its ability to meet contractual arrangements. “The impact of port congestion and delays is widespread across the automotive manufacturing value chain,” Renai Moothilal, chief executive officer at the National Association of Automotive Component and Allied Manufacturers, said in reply to questions. “These are detrimental to the competitiveness of the value proposition for South African automotive manufacturers.” Durban Gateway Terminal, the operator majority-owned by ICTSI, said it took the concerns of Metair and others seriously, and will meet Naacam’s members on Monday to discuss the disruptions.

items.original_title: US court orders arrest of tanker after New Orleans cruise ship collision
items.summary: A US federal court has authorised the arrest of the tanker Atlantic Asphalt after the Port of New Orleans launched legal action seeking more than $1m in damages following the collision that sank American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage. The Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans filed the lawsuit in the Eastern District of Louisiana, naming the tanker, its owner Nave Shipping SA and OSM Thome’s Singapore-based Thome Ship Management as defendants. The port alleges that the collision caused extensive damage to its Thalia Street Terminal, where American Heritage was berthed. Physical damage is currently estimated to exceed $1m, with additional claims expected for cleanup, surveys, repairs and salvage. A federal judge subsequently authorised the arrest of Atlantic Asphalt , issuing a warrant directing US marshals to take possession of the vessel and hold it subject to further court orders. The 17,764 dwt asphalt tanker struck American Heritage on November 13 , causing the river cruise ship to capsize and partially sink. The lawsuit alleges negligence by the tanker interests, although the cause of the collision remains under investigation. OSM Thome confirmed that it manages Atlantic Asphalt and said the vessel was stable at anchor following the incident. The company said it had activated its emergency response team and was cooperating fully with local authorities.

items.title: EU Emission Trading System applying to offshore vessels from 1 January 2027
items.original_title: EU Emission Trading System applying to offshore vessels from 1 January 2027
items.summary: Introduction From 1 January 2027, the application of the EU ETS Directive (EU ETS)[2] will extend to include offshore vessels of 5,000 GT or above. Already, since 1 January 2026, the maritime scope of EU ETS has not only included CO₂ emissions alone, but also methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) emission. So, from 2027 onwards offshore shipping companies will have to surrender EU Allowances (EUAs) in respect of CO₂, methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions for all their ships that call at a port within the EEA commercially. If an offshore vessel calls at an EEA port for non-commercial reasons, e.g., obtaining supplies, a ship being in need of assistance or in distress, taking shelter from adverse weather, or it being rendered necessary by search and rescue activities, etc., then such port call is not deemed to be a ‘port of call’ for the purposes of the EU ETS, provided that no commercial operation takes place during that same call.

Dry freight has continued its recovery, crude oil has softened further and regional steel prices have offered some encouragement. Recycling indications remain unchanged across all four destinations, with healthy buying interest still frustrated by the persistent shortage of available candidates. Dry freight provided the week’s clearest movement. The Baltic Dry Index advanced to 3,020 on Thursday, November 12, from 2,740 a week earlier, extending its recovery to seven consecutive sessions. For buyers awaiting a sustained freight correction, the market has once again moved in the opposite direction. For now, the beaches have the interest and the capacity. The trading market still has the upper hand. For Week 46 of 2026, GMS Market Rankings / Vessel indications are as below.

items.title: Resistance for shipping’s record rally
items.original_title: Resistance for shipping’s record rally
items.summary: The report examines whether investors are right to assume that today’s record profitability will fade. Its conclusion is that while much of the additional shipping demand generated by geopolitical disruption appears durable, but some of the most lucrative sectors, particularly crude tankers, remain highly exposed to a sudden reversal. The current market strength is unprecedented in duration. As the report notes, “buyers are paying for months of record earnings, not years”. For LPG carriers, an average round voyage that took 41 days in 2019 now requires 55 days, reducing annual cargo-carrying productivity by roughly a quarter. For VLCCs, suezmaxes, capesizes and large gas carriers, the orderbook exceeds the entire fleet of vessels older than 20 years. A ten-year-old VLCC could lose up to 65% of its value under such a scenario, while a 15-year-old unit could lose more than 80%. Around 1,800 vessels across the five major segments are employed solely because round trips have become longer than they were before 2019. “Almost half of the extra work looks set to last,” yet at the same time, “the top layer could go within weeks”, particularly for crude tankers.

items.title: Tanker Market Surged in October
items.original_title: Tanker Market Surged in October
items.summary: Suezmax spot freight rates experienced the largest increase, m-o-m, of the three major vessel classes. On the USGC-to-Europe route, Suezmax rates rose 139%, m-o-m. Compared to the same period last year, spot freight rates were seven times higher. Very large crude carriers (VLCC) VLCC spot freight rates were the key drive of the tanker market in October, with record high rates pressuring Suezmax, Aframax and even the clean tanker market. Compared with the same month in 2025, rates were over four times higher on both routes. Clean tanker freight rates The clean tanker market began to see some pressure from the exceptionally high rates in the dirty market in October. In October, West of Suez spot freight rates increased 95%, m-o-m, on average, and were up 168% compared to the same month last year. East of Suez spot rates rose 30%, m-o-m, building on the sharp increase seen in the previous month and were six-times higher, y-o-y. Compared with October 2025, rates were almost eight times higher.

items.title: One State-Owned Manager, Three Vessels, Three Subsea Cable Corridors in One Week
items.original_title: One State-Owned Manager, Three Vessels, Three Subsea Cable Corridors in One Week
items.summary: Between October 15 and November 4, 2026, three vessels under the same state-owned Xiamen manager stopped on three international submarine cable corridors in three different seas. A Chinese-flagged research vessel operated by a Chinese university spent nearly three weeks on survey stations in and around the SJC2 and EAC-C2C corridors east of Taiwan, then 3.5 days on a line of stations across SJC2 that took it into Japan’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ), where Japan’s coast guard observed it lowering a wire into the sea. In the same week, a second research vessel operated by a separate Chinese university went dark twice and reappeared on the SEA-H2X corridor in the South China Sea, and a Hong Kong-flagged bulk carrier managed by the same subsidiary loitered for about 31 hours over the Pacific Light Cable Network (PLCN) in the western Pacific. It stayed almost stationary for about 5 hours inside the cable corridor and loitered in the area for about 31 hours, then drifted north and resumed its voyage west at 11 knots at 09:40 UTC on November 4. The close-up shows the 31-hour stop in and around the PLCN corridor on November 3–4, 2026. The Common Thread: One State-Owned Manager The three vessels sit under a single Xiamen-based ship management subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned enterprise listed in Shanghai.

items.title: New Intl Smart Shipping Alliance launched in Shanghai
items.original_title: New Intl Smart Shipping Alliance launched in Shanghai
items.summary: The International Smart Shipping Alliance (ISSA) has been officially established in Shanghai, with an initial membership of nine. The Shanghai Marine Equipment Research Institute of China State Shipbuilding Corp Ltd (CSSC) is the only ship research institute among the founding members, highlighting the growing influence of China’s ship research capabilities. The alliance was jointly initiated by Shanghai Maritime University and the Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO), with its secretariat based at Shanghai Maritime University. The ISSA is a non-profit international industry alliance that brings together industry participants across the entire industrial chain, including technology, ships, regulations, operations and applications. Guided by the principles of safety, compliance, openness, collaboration and sustainability, the ISSA was established as the global shipping industry increasingly integrates intelligent technologies. An action plan on intelligent shipping was jointly issued by four Chinese government departments, including the Ministry of Transport, targeting more than five trial shipping routes, over 10 typical application scenarios and more than 100 intelligent ships by 2030. Source: China Daily

items.title: Gulf Oil Exports Recover as Hormuz Shipping Struggles
items.original_title: Gulf Oil Exports Recover as Hormuz Shipping Struggles
items.summary: FILE PHOTO: Oil/Chemical Tanker "Bald Man" at the Port of Fujairah, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, May 6, 2026. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo Global oil markets are beginning to recover from the Iran war, but shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted, with vessel traffic roughly 65% below pre-conflict levels and tanker attacks continuing across the region. Separate reports released Friday by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) highlight the uneven recovery in energy trade nearly nine months after the conflict began. The IEA said global oil supplies are on track to exceed demand by 1.7 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, reversing its previous forecast of a deficit as Persian Gulf producers restore disrupted exports. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, climbed to 18.4 million barrels per day in October, just 26% below pre-war levels. The recovery in Gulf exports is beginning to ease pressure on global oil markets. The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping.

items.title: World Oil Market is Returning to Surplus as Gulf Exports Recover
items.original_title: World Oil Market is Returning to Surplus as Gulf Exports Recover
items.summary: The Malta-flagged tanker Agios Fanourios I, an oil tanker that sailed through the Strait of Hormuz, arrives in Iraq’s territorial waters off Basra,Iraq April 17, 2026. REUTERS/Mohammed Aty LONDON, Nov 13 – The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping. The agency also gave more details of remaining volumes to come from a record release of oil from its members’ emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71 million barrels would be made available by the end of February including 15 million barrels of diesel to ease market tightness. “The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” the agency said in the report. The report follows signs that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports disrupted since the start of the war in late February by using workarounds such as so-called dark crossings through the Strait of Hormuz, where tankers switch off tracking signals to evade attack.

items.title: CMA CGM Net Profit More Than Triples to $2.32 Billion as Freight Rates Surge
items.original_title: CMA CGM Net Profit More Than Triples to $2.32 Billion as Freight Rates Surge
items.summary: French shipping giant CMA CGM more than tripled its third-quarter net profit as higher container freight rates and strong cargo volumes boosted earnings amid ongoing disruptions to global shipping routes in the Middle East. The Marseille-based group reported Friday that net income attributable to the group climbed to $2.32 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up from $760 million a year earlier, an increase of approximately 205%. Revenue rose 31.1% to $18.4 billion, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) jumped 61.6% to $4.78 billion. The strong results were driven primarily by CMA CGM’s container shipping business, which benefited from sustained demand and elevated freight rates as Middle East tensions continued to disrupt maritime trade routes and global supply chains. The figures underscore how ongoing disruptions in the Middle East are reshaping the container shipping market, supporting freight rates even as carriers face longer voyages, higher operating costs and changes to established trade routes. CMA CGM also expanded its terminal network through a partnership involving Terminal 4 at Saudi Arabia’s Port of Jeddah and the acquisition of a 49% stake in Morocco’s Nador Container Terminal. Looking ahead, CMA CGM expects strong container shipping demand to continue over the coming months , with freight rates that have been rising since the second quarter supporting the business.

items.summary: FILE PHOTO: A Russian national flag flies behind a sign bearing the logo of Rosneft oil company installed at a fuel station in Saint Petersburg, Russia, October 23, 2025. REUTERS/Anton Vaganov/File Photo Nov 13, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Russia’s October revenues from crude and petroleum-product exports hit the highest since May as the ongoing Iran war bolstered oil prices, according to the International Energy Agency. Russian oil producers earned almost $21.2 billion in export revenue last month, up about 65% from a year earlier, the IEA said in a report Friday. Crude accounted for more than 80% of the total, as the nation’s petroleum-product output and exports were pressured by Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries. The country’s key crude blends, Urals and ESPO, topped $100 a barrel last month due to hostilities in the Middle East, with near daily attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and intense strikes by Houthis on Saudi energy infrastructure, the agency said. Last month, net budget revenues from oil levies totaled around $10 billion, dented by multi-billion-ruble payouts to support domestic fuel deliveries, Bloomberg calculations based on Finance Ministry data show.

items.title: Blanked sailings on the rise, with container spot rates on a gentle decline
items.original_title: Blanked sailings on the rise, with container spot rates on a gentle decline
items.summary: Container spot freight rates on the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades saw another week of gentle declines amid reduced demand post-peak season, while Asia-Europe carriers and their customers begin annual contract negotiations in earnest. This week’s World Container Index (WCI) from Drewry saw spot rates on its Shanghai-Rotterdam leg decline 3% week on week, to $3,504 per 40ft, while pricing on the Shanghai-Genoa route remained flat for the third week in a row, at $4,168 per 40ft. A new round of FAK (freight all kinds) levels are set to be applied next week, although they are modest in ambition and generally range from $4,500-$5,000 per 40ft on Asia-North Europe shipments, and between $5,500-$6,600 per 40ft on Asia-Mediterranean. However, they are also being accompanied by increased number of blanked sailings – according to Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight, eight are scheduled for next week, compared with the five this week. The key aspect to this is that carriers and their customers are positioning for next year, with carriers keen to get spot rates up as much as they can to act as a guide for contract rates, and shippers are, understandably, eager for them to be suppressed after enduring a wild ride during much of 2026.

items.title: Germany’s 2027 budget spares rail terminals, but locks in ‘painful’ track subsidy cuts
items.original_title: Germany’s 2027 budget spares rail terminals, but locks in ‘painful’ track subsidy cuts
items.summary: Germany’s 2027 budget passed its final committee stage overnight, leaving most of the cuts to rail freight support untouched. Terminal funding escaped, but track access subsidies did not, with operators stating they are ‘utterly baffled’ by why, after fierce campaigning, they still face a claimed 75% jump in network costs from next month. The Bundestag’s budget committee approved the 2027 federal budget in the early hours of Friday 13 November, after a session that ran until 5:55am, ahead of a final vote by the full parliament later this month. The cuts were first unveiled in the federal government’s summer draft budget in July, triggering four months of intense lobbying by rail freight groups to overturn them in parliament. “Knowingly burdening users in industry and trade and encouraging the shift to road is short-sighted and an affront to businesses and people alike.” The broader €25.35 billion transport budget saw steep cuts elsewhere, however, with 2027 investments for federal highway operator Autobahn GmbH slashed by €1.98 billion to €2.38 billion, alongside a €5.5 billion reduction in future commitment authorisations. Prior to the vote, terminal operator Contargo , together with members of combined transport research body SGKV, had called for at least €120 million in 2027 and €150 million in 2028, plus significantly higher commitments for 2028 to 2030.

items.summary: Nanning is seeking to transform itself from an inland Chinese city into an international logistics hub serving South-east Asia, leveraging Pinglu Canal’s September opening to strengthen river-sea connectivity. It also wants to expand trade links with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). The capital of Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region is accelerating the development of an integrated transport network spanning road, rail, waterways, and air, with the canal expected to play a pivotal role in connecting inland cargo flows to international shipping routes. Yesterday, Nanning municipal officials outlined the plans, with Municipal Bureau of Commerce deputy director Wu Shaopeng noting: “With the Pinglu Canal’s opening, Nanning port has evolved from primarily handling domestic trade into a departure point for river-sea intermodal transport.” At the Baliang joint operation area, in the Liujing Port district, berths 1 to 6 have opened to foreign trade, allowing international cargo to be imported and exported directly through the port. The city’s expressway network now exceeds 1,500 km, while the Nanning International Railway Port operates daily cross-border rail freight services to Vietnam. Nanning Wuxu International Airport has an annual cargo and mail handling capacity of 400,000 tonnes, and operates seven international cargo routes serving ASEAN markets.

items.title: Democrat success may mean more trade stability, but alongside tariffs
items.original_title: Democrat success may mean more trade stability, but alongside tariffs
items.summary: Following the Democrats’ midterm US election victories, freight forwarders and importers could face greater stability in trade policy, but little immediate relief from existing duties. Nunzio De Filipis, co-CEO of CargoTrans, told The Loadstar Podcast the election result could slow the pace of tariff changes, although he expects the duties to remain. “I don’t think we’re going to see the lever being pushed as fast as it has been,” he said, adding: “But I don’t see them going away.” He pointed to the survival of Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods through successive administrations, noting that President Joe Biden had retained and expanded measures introduced during Donald Trump’s first term. Reuters reported this month that Democratic control of Congress would provide greater opportunities to scrutinise President Trump’s trade agenda, but noted that lawmakers faced significant obstacles to repealing tariffs, including presidential veto powers and existing executive trade authority. Similarly, the legislative and regulatory advisory arm of professional services firm EY explained in its recent trade policy alert that Democratic control would shift congressional committee leadership and increase oversight of trade policy. However, the advisory noted that the election result would not itself change the tariffs or presidential trade powers, while substantial legislative changes would still require sufficient Congressional support ,and either President Trump’s signature or a veto-proof majority.

items.title: Forwarders need to be specialists to make pharma work
items.original_title: Forwarders need to be specialists to make pharma work
items.summary: SME forwarders looking to enter pharmaceutical logistics should avoid competing directly with multinationals and instead focus on building specialist capabilities, says Pharma.Aero secretary general Frank van Gelder. Rising demand from clinical trials and time-critical healthcare shipments, together with the emergence of advanced therapies, is creating opportunities for SMEs, but Mr van Gelder said operators must demonstrate the requisite expertise, systems quality and dependability. He told The Loadstar : “SME forwarders should become indispensable specialists. Emerging connections with Chinese and Indian innovation ecosystems can create further possibilities, provided operators build real expertise rather than simply market a new lane.” But he warned forwarders off entering the pharma market simply because of the prospect of attractive margins. GDP compliance, qualified personnel, validated procedures, and temperature-control competence were needed to form the foundations of any operation. Compete on expertise, reliability, flexibility, and trust.” This, he added, included an ability to respond to disruption, which offered SMEs a way to distinguish themselves. Workforce resilience, he said, meant giving employees the confidence and authority to raise concerns and act when contingency plans no longer worked. “Resilience is not created by a contingency plan. It is created by people who can act when that plan no longer works,”

items.title: Singapore Retains Maritime City “Crown”, as Piraeus Jumps Up the Ranks
items.original_title: Singapore Retains Maritime City “Crown”, as Piraeus Jumps Up the Ranks
items.summary: The maritime industry enters 2026 after another period of disruption and adjustment. Trade remains active, but the conditions supporting it have become more demanding. Singapore remains the world’s leading maritime city in 2026. Compared with the 2024 ranking, Singapore retains first place, while Shanghai moves up from fourth to second. London’s results demonstrate that a leading maritime city does not need to control the largest fleet or port. Athens rises to 13th place globally, retaining its position as the world’s second-strongest shipping hub Athens records one of the most significant improvements in the global ranking of maritime cities, climbing from 35th place in 2024 to 13th in 2026. The city ranks third globally in the adoption of energy-saving technologies across its fleet, behind Taipei and Imabari. In addition, Athens ranks second worldwide in the size of its owner-controlled fleet capable of using lower-carbon-intensive fuels, with approximately 3.3 million gross tonnes, compared with 5.1 million for Singapore. Busan ranks second in Maritime Technology and remains the leading shipbuilding hub, including for vessels capable of using lower-carbon-intensive fuels.

items.title: MPA Opens Applications for LNG Floating Storage Unit Licences in Singapore
items.original_title: MPA Opens Applications for LNG Floating Storage Unit Licences in Singapore
items.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) has opened applications for licences to operate up to two liquefied natural gas (LNG) Floating Storage Units (FSUs) in Singapore anchorages. The call for applications follows MPA’s award of eight new LNG bunker supplier licences in July 2026[1]. To support the continued growth of LNG bunkering services in Singapore and strengthen supply resilience, the FSUs will complement the expanded supplier base by diversifying LNG storage and reloading options. Key FSU Licensing Requirements Applications are open to existing LNG bunker licensees, who may partner third-party terminal operators to provide the necessary storage and operational expertise. Most of the FSU’s storage capacity must be allocated for LNG bunkering and there will be a minimum requirement for capacity that must be made available to other LNG bunker suppliers on open-access terms. Applicants must own or charter at least one FSU with a minimum storage capacity of 130,000 m³, registered with the Singapore Registry of Ships, and comply with MPA’s safety and operational requirements. FSU operators must also disclose to MPA the intended maximum fees chargeable for LNG reloading services. This will enable the infrastructure to support the supply of these lower-emission LNG alternatives as they become more widely available. Source: Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore

items.title: Iron Ore Slides Toward Four-Year Low
items.original_title: Iron Ore Slides Toward Four-Year Low
items.summary: Iron ore futures declined to around CNY 670 per ton, approaching their lowest levels since October 2022 as rising supply and weakening demand continued to weigh on the market. Industry data showed that iron ore inventories at major Chinese ports increased for another week, with Brazilian shipments contributing to the buildup for a fourth consecutive week. Demand prospects were further dampened by anticipated production restrictions across key steelmaking hubs in China’s Hebei province. Major steel-producing cities, including Tangshan and Handan, have entered the autumn-winter air pollution control period, during which unfavorable weather conditions have periodically disrupted sintering operations and blast furnace utilization. Meanwhile, industry figures indicated that average hot metal output among Chinese steelmakers, a key gauge of iron ore demand, continued to decline, adding further pressure to prices. Source: Trading Economics

Jens Grunenberg, Lloyd’s Register’s Germany Commercial Manager, discusses why local expertise remains critical in an increasingly global industry, how German maritime businesses are navigating rapid change, and why close relationships continue to matter when making complex technical and commercial decisions. In such an international industry, that local connection and cultural understanding is something customers still highly appreciate.

items.title: Chinese-backed Simandou iron ore project in Guinea makes major progress
items.original_title: Chinese-backed Simandou iron ore project in Guinea makes major progress
items.summary: China Baowu Steel Group (CBSG) announced on Thursday that the north section of the Simandou iron ore and infrastructure project in Guinea, a world-class hematite deposit, has been completed and entered operation. Industry observers said that the achievement marks the diversification of China’s iron ore import sources and highlights the growing capability of Chinese companies in global resource development and integrated project delivery. The mine project, operated by the Chinese-backed Baowu Winning Consortium Simandou, has completed the full-line heavy-load trial run of its second series downhill conveyor system. The Simandou project officially commenced operations in Guinea in November 2025. Located in southeastern Guinea in west Africa, the Simandou deposit stretches about 110 kilometers along a mountain range. According to customs data, China imported about 1.26 billion tons of iron ore in 2025, setting a record after three consecutive years of growth. In the first three quarters of this year, China imported 10.08 million tons of iron ore from Guinea, placing the West African country among China’s top 10 iron ore import sources, according to China’s General Administration of Customs. Analysts said that once the Simandou iron ore project reaches full production, its output will account for about 5 percent of global iron ore supply, equivalent to nearly 10 percent of China’s annual iron ore imports.

items.title: From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping
items.original_title: From ocean liner to artificial reef: A warning for container shipping
items.summary: Dr Raymon Krishnan, president of Singapore’s Logistics & Supply Chain Management Society, writes for Splash today, reflecting on one of this week’s most talked about stories in the mainstream press. On Wednesday, the 990-foot ocean liner SS United States was deliberately sunk off Destin, Florida, to become what is expected to be the world’s largest artificial reef. Initial underwater inspections found the vessel upright, approximately 180 feet below the surface. Its retirement offers a useful perspective on container shipping as it now faces another turning point. The container shipping industry is preparing for a significant increase in fleet capacity. According to Drewry’s third-quarter 2026 Container Forecaster the global containership orderbook stood at approximately 13.9m teu on 1 September 2026, equivalent to 40.9% of the active fleet. Aviation permanently changed the market for passenger liners, while container shipping remains essential to trade. Conversion into an artificial reef offers a potential tourism and conservation role but it is neither a universal nor necessarily economical solution for commercial vessels. It is to ensure there is a commercially sustainable reason to put them to work.

Otynshiyev has been leading KTZ since July. He was appointed by the head of Samruk-Kazyna, the country’s sovereign wealth fund, Nurlan Zhakupov, who owns the railway company. Otynshiyev is also the Chairman of the Managing Board of TITR, the company managing the Middle Corridor. The arrests were carried out on Wednesday, 11 November by Kazakhstan’s Anti-Corruption Service of the National Security Committee. “No further information regarding the progress of the pre-trial investigation may be disclosed”, the Kazakh government explained. KTZ is the main rail operator in Kazakhstan for freight and passenger services. The company plays a vital role in being a bridge between China and Europe along two of the three main rail routes connecting the two, including the Middle Corridor.

items.summary: BW LPG has struck another lucrative vessel sale, offloading a VLGC acquired in John Fredriksen’s Avance Gas fleet deal less than two years ago for well over $100m. The New York- and Oslo-listed gas carrier giant has agreed to sell the 2015-built, 83,134 cu m BW Mistral , with the transaction expected to generate a net book gain of around $37m and net cash proceeds of approximately $104m. Built at China’s Jiangnan shipyard, the scrubber-fitted vessel is currently trading in the spot market and will continue earning revenue for BW LPG until its scheduled handover by mid-January 2027. The disposal marks another profitable exit from the 12-ship Avance Gas fleet acquired in August 2024 for $1.05bn in cash, shares and assumed debt. In July, BW LPG agreed to sell the 2015-built, 83,000 cu m BW Levant , another vessel from the Avance transaction, with expected net cash proceeds of $38m and a book gain of around $17m. The two deals are set to generate combined book gains of approximately $54m and net cash proceeds of $142m. The latest sale comes amid a broader fleet renewal drive at BW LPG.

items.title: Cetus seals $200m share placement ahead of Oslo debut
items.original_title: Cetus seals $200m share placement ahead of Oslo debut
items.summary: Hong Kong-based dry bulk owner Cetus Maritime has successfully placed a NOK1.89bn ($200m) share offering, including an over-allotment, clearing a major hurdle ahead of its planned Oslo stock market debut next week. The Mark Young-led company said it had conditionally allocated 108.5m shares at NOK17.44 ($1.83) apiece, taking up the full $25m over-allotment on top of its original $175m fundraising target. The transaction comprises 95m new shares raising approximately $174m for Cetus, alongside 13.5m existing shares borrowed from major shareholder Pacific Transportation Asia (PTA) to cover the over-allotment. The proceeds should help fund Cetus’s acquisition of 13 handysize and ultramax bulkers from Hong Kong-listed Seacon Shipping Group, along with Syngrace, which holds contracts for three additional handysize newbuildings. The transaction involves approximately $72.5m in cash and the issuance of 37.3m Cetus shares to Seacon. Following completion of the fleet acquisition and a planned vessel sale, Cetus said it expects to operate 42 ships, comprising 34 vessels on the water and eight newbuildings scheduled for delivery in 2027 and 2028. The company is targeting November 18 for its first day of trading on Euronext Growth Oslo, subject to regulatory approvals and completion of the Seacon transaction. Cetus has also left the door open for a move to the main Oslo Børs list within 12 months of its debut.

items.title: UK blacklists 11 ships in fresh Russia sanctions sweep
items.original_title: UK blacklists 11 ships in fresh Russia sanctions sweep
items.summary: Britain has slapped fresh sanctions on 11 ships linked to Russian energy exports, targeting five LNG carriers, five oil tankers and a floating storage unit in its latest effort to disrupt Moscow’s seaborne oil and gas trade. The measures also cover nine companies, including Russian oil producer Slavneft, Rosneft’s Vostok Oil project and several energy trading businesses based in Dubai. The latest vessel additions include LNG carriers Melicertes, Neleus, Perle, Aeolus and Oneiroi , alongside the Novatek-linked Koryak FSU . The restrictions prohibit the specified ships from accessing British ports and impose controls on chartering and operating them. Dubai-based Forteza Trading, Patera and Novus Energy have been designated, with British authorities specifically linking Novus Energy to dealings involving vessels already subject to UK restrictions. Russian petrochemical producer Sibur and coal groups SUEK and Kuzbassrazrezugol also feature in the latest package. The move brings all ten of Russia’s largest oil producers under British sanctions following the inclusion of Slavneft. The government announced the measures during the European Political Community summit in Dublin, where pressure on Russian energy revenues formed part of discussions on Ukraine. Britain has been steadily expanding its maritime restrictions this year, including sanctions against six ships in August and an earlier package targeting Russia’s developing LNG shadow fleet.

items.title: HSL launches Amsterdam-Germany service to battle low Rhine levels
items.original_title: HSL launches Amsterdam-Germany service to battle low Rhine levels
items.summary: German operator HSL has added rail capacity between Amsterdam and Germany’s Rhine-Neckar region to make up for barges hampered by low water on the Rhine. The services, running since the end of October, carry bulk goods, liquid fuels and petroleum products, with coal trains hauling up to 4,000 tonnes each. “With these new services, we are helping industry in the Rhine-Neckar region to compensate for the loss of inland waterway transport capacity and to maintain the supply of raw materials even during periods of low water on the Rhine”, said Stefan Frankowski, Managing Director of HSL Logistik GmbH. To reach the 4,000-tonne mark, the coal trains run with double-unit traction, with two locomotives hauling each convoy. However, HSL did not disclose how many trains per week are running or the total volumes it expects to carry. In August, DB Cargo said it could mobilise around 400 wagons at short notice, while Captrain added up to 13,600 tonnes of weekly coal and coke capacity. Logistics company VTG said in October that the German network cannot absorb all the cargo diverted from the river, partly due to maintenance works. On top of that, the right-bank Rhine line between Troisdorf and Wiesbaden is closed for renovation until mid-December.

items.title: Baltic Exchange and Mercuria await verdict in landmark tanker index trial
items.original_title: Baltic Exchange and Mercuria await verdict in landmark tanker index trial
items.summary: One of shipping’s most consequential legal battles has concluded in London, with the Baltic Exchange and commodities trader Mercuria awaiting a High Court ruling on whether the industry’s leading VLCC freight benchmark should have continued operating after war erupted in the Middle East. At the centre of the dispute is TD3C, the Baltic’s benchmark for transporting crude from Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia to Ningbo, China, a voyage requiring passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Mercuria has argued that the disruption following the outbreak of hostilities on February 28 rendered the benchmark unreliable, with insufficient physical tanker activity to support meaningful assessments. The trading house maintains that the Baltic failed to meet its statutory and contractual obligations by continuing to publish rates despite mounting evidence that its contributing shipbrokers could not reliably determine a market price. During the trial, Mercuria highlighted internal communications revealing considerable uncertainty among Baltic staff and broker panellists. In closing arguments, the Baltic accused Mercuria of repeatedly changing its case and suggested the litigation was an attempt to escape the consequences of unsuccessful trading positions. The Baltic has also warned that retrospective intervention in a widely used benchmark could create significant uncertainty for freight derivatives and physical shipping contracts linked to TD3C. The Baltic Exchange has consistently defended its benchmark procedures and regulatory compliance.

The work will examine existing railheads and sidings, potential new sites, network access and the commercial viability of additional rail-based services. It will also assess the wider economic, social and environmental benefits of developing rail freight infrastructure. North Lincolnshire already has significant rail freight activity, particularly associated with the ports and industrial facilities around the Humber. Immingham is an established centre for bulk and other freight movements, while existing rail infrastructure provides connections to the wider national network. It will examine network access and operational requirements, as well as whether proposed facilities could support commercially viable rail freight movements. The freight study is scheduled to run until June 2027. Its findings will establish whether new or improved rail freight infrastructure is practical, commercially beneficial and consistent with local priorities, such as the continued presence of steel-making at Scunthorpe . items.title: Singapore-flagged cargo ship strikes US bridge
items.original_title: Singapore-flagged cargo ship strikes US bridge
items.summary: A Singapore-flagged cargoship has struck a bridge spanning the Delaware River between Philadelphia and New Jersey, forcing its closure and renewing concerns about the vulnerability of American bridges to vessel collisions. The 180 m Strategic Alliance, a handysize bulk carrier built in 2013, hit the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge at approximately 1.15pm local time on Thursday while its draw span was open for marine traffic. The impact damaged part of the bridge and initially prevented the structure from closing, causing extensive traffic delays on both sides of the river. The vessel subsequently moored at a Kinder Morgan terminal in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where US Coast Guard inspectors attended. The bridge, which opened in 1929 and carries up to 76,200 vehicles daily, reopened around 8.40pm, with one lane remaining closed for repairs. The incident comes as American authorities seek to strengthen protection for bridges following the March 2024 Dali disaster in Baltimore, when a containership, also Singapore-flagged, struck the Francis Scott Key Bridge, causing its collapse and killing six construction workers. In September, the US Coast Guard published a major review examining bridge and port infrastructure vulnerabilities across 11 ports, producing 20 recommendations for improving maritime risk management. Maryland is also pursuing a $177m programme to strengthen the Chesapeake Bay Bridge against ship strikes, including new protective structures around its supporting piers.

As ships remain in service for longer, the dry bulk fleet has gradually aged, with the average bulk carrier now over 13 years old, compared with an average of 10 years at the start of the decade,” says Gouveia. There are now 1,035 dry bulk ships, totalling 46.7m DWT, which are more than 25 years old. In our latest Dry Bulk Shipping Market Overview & Outlook, we forecast the supply/demand balance to gradually weaken in 2027 and 2028, albeit from a high baseline. Ship deliveries are expected to accelerate, growing 19% in 2027 and a further 4% in 2028. Consequently, we estimate ship recycling could increase to 5.5m DWT in 2027 and 9.2m DWT in 2028, which would be the highest since 2020. Loading tanks aboard the ‘Brisbane Star’ at the Port of Newport in 1942 Preserving our maritime history This history continues to be recognised today.
